scenario: Six of today's 8 papers are about LLM inference serving. llm-d 1.0 handles agent traffic with prefix-cache-aware routing and separate prefill and decode. deep_reading.title: llm-d 1.0, an open source stack for distributed inference
deep_reading.content:
A year ago, most inference traffic was still chat: one prompt in, one response out. Now more and more requests come from multi-step agents and reinforcement-learning rollouts, which fan out across several tools, share very long prefixes and arrive in bursts. Put this traffic on a single machine, or behind an ordinary round-robin load balancer, and the replicas recompute the same prompts, accelerator memory fills up with duplicate KV cache, and one bursty agent loop can stall interactive users' requests. llm-d 1.0, released at the PyTorch Conference by Google together with Red Hat, IBM and others, is an open-source distributed inference stack that runs on Kubernetes and organizes a set of vLLM and SGLang model servers into one serving pool. The router knows which replicas hold each cached prefix and sends a session's requests back to them. When accelerator memory runs short, KV cache is moved to host memory and storage, and high-priority requests can jump the queue. On an agentic coding workload on Ironwood TPU, prefix-aware routing plus host-memory offload cut median time-to-first-token (TTFT) by more than 85% and delivered 2.4x the total throughput of a plain Kubernetes Service. ==Most of these gains come from no longer recomputing prefixes that have already been computed, not from faster kernels==.

This is a Google Cloud product blog, read together with IBM Research's introduction from the same day. Below, I first explain the problem llm-d solves, then break down four components, routing, KV-cache tiering, prefill/decode disaggregation and flow control, and finally look at the production numbers the blog gives. All numbers come from these two blogs, and most of them come without a full experimental setup.

## 1. The problem: why agent traffic breaks ordinary load balancing

![The three stages of llm-d's evolution (Google blog Figure 1). On the left is an ordinary Kubernetes Service that hands requests round-robin to model servers that each do both prefill and decode; in the middle, a cache- and load-aware router is added, prefill and decode pools are separated, and KV cache is split into three tiers, accelerator memory, CPU memory and storage; on the right, flow control is added to the router, queuing requests in three tiers, free, standard and high priority. The components that appear from left to right are exactly what 1.0 does beyond an ordinary deployment.](figs/google-llmd-1.0-2026-10-20/fig1_evolution.png)

LLM inference has two steps: prefill reads the whole prompt once and computes the KV cache for every token; decode then generates new tokens one by one from that cache. The compute of prefill grows with prompt length. An agent calls the model many times within one task, and every prompt contains the same system instructions, code and conversation history, with only a few new turns appended at the end.

If the second call is sent round-robin to a different replica, that replica has no cache from the first call and has to prefill the whole prefix again. The more replicas there are, the lower the chance of landing on the original one. IBM's blog puts it directly: if every step requires the model to reread the same material, you are repeatedly paying for work the system has already done.

The second problem is mixed load. Interactive requests need low latency, background agent loops and RL rollouts need throughput, and demand swings by the minute. Without priorities, interactive requests queue behind a large batch of background requests.

## 2. Method: four components

The first component is the router, which looks at where cache lives when it picks a replica. It is built on the Gateway API Inference extension for Kubernetes, tracks which replicas hold each cached prefix, and weighs that information together with replica load and predicted latency when choosing a replica. Version 1.0 adds three agent-oriented features. Session-aware routing sends later requests in a session back to the same replica where possible. Turn-priority scheduling is the second, though the blog does not say how priority depends on the turn. The third is native Responses API state at the routing layer, so later requests need only reference the previous response's ID instead of resending the whole history, with the server filling in the earlier context. In IBM's words, multi-turn requests stay pinned to the appropriate replicas, so their prefix caches stay usable.

The second component handles KV cache that no longer fits in accelerator memory. Once that memory is full, llm-d does not simply drop old cache; it uses vLLM's OffloadingConnector, Mooncake or SGLang's HiCache to move it to host memory, and further down to SSD or Google Cloud Managed Lustre. ==This is meant to avoid many prefixes being pushed out of accelerator memory at once under multi-turn, long-context load and then recomputed all together==; the blog calls this a prefix-eviction storm.

The third component separates prefill from decode. Prefill is compute-heavy and decode is bound by memory bandwidth, so running both on the same replicas makes each wait on the other. llm-d therefore splits prefill, decode and multimodal encode into separate pools, and uses wide expert parallelism to spread large MoE models across nodes: experts are spread over many GPUs on several nodes, each holding only a few, and each token is sent to the GPUs holding the experts it selects. DisaggregatedSet, new in 1.0 and built on LeaderWorkerSet, the Kubernetes API for multi-host inference, manages these pools as one unit: during rolling updates, prefill and decode move together to matching versions, while scaling stays independent for each.

The fourth component handles queuing. Flow control queues requests by priority and fairness, so latency-sensitive requests and bursty agent workloads can share one set of hardware without starving each other. Version 1.0 also adds llm-d-async-processor, which pulls latency-tolerant requests from queues such as Pub/Sub or Redis and routes them alongside real-time traffic, but runs them only on spare capacity and enforces strict priority lanes and quotas.

![The full stack on Google Cloud (Google blog Figure 2). From top to bottom: 1,000 agents running in Agent Substrate sandboxes; llm-d's multi-node orchestration layer, including the router, flow control, tiered KV cache and prefill/decode disaggregation; the single-node model engines vLLM, SGLang and TorchTPU; and TPU hardware at the bottom. Look at the division of labor between the middle two layers: llm-d handles only cross-node scheduling, and single-node performance is left to the inference engines.](figs/google-llmd-1.0-2026-10-20/fig2_stack.png)

This figure also shows where llm-d sits. It does not replace vLLM or SGLang; it sits in front of them and does the scheduling. ==Teams can keep their existing inference engine, models and cluster, and plug in only the components they need==; the order the blog recommends is to first add prefix-aware routing in front of an existing vLLM deployment, then add flow control, KV-cache offloading and prefill/decode disaggregation.

## 3. What is new in 1.0

IBM's blog points out that the five techniques, prefix-cache-aware routing, KV-cache offloading, batch inference optimization, prefill/decode disaggregation and wide expert parallelism, existed before 1.0; what changes in 1.0 is that they can run long-term as a critical service. Specifically:

- Multi-tenant quality of service: flow control by priority and fairness.
- Stability: the APIs move to v1 with a stability promise, and the path a request takes from the router to the inference engine has been hardened. The team says this was validated on multiple clouds and accelerator types but does not list which problems were fixed.
- Safer upgrades: router high availability, zero-downtime updates, and the DisaggregatedSet described above.
- Agent-aware serving: session-aware routing, turn-priority scheduling and native Responses API state.
- TPU support: TorchTPU runs PyTorch models natively on TPUs inside vLLM and SGLang, with cooperative time-slicing.

Time-slicing targets idle time in RL training. The blog says that during rollout generation or weight updates, accelerators sit idle 40% to 60% of the time; llm-d fits async inference into these gaps, raising aggregate accelerator duty cycles from a baseline of about 40% to more than 70%.

## 4. Experiments and production numbers

The blog's numbers fall into two kinds: Google's own tests and production traffic, and user reports. Each set gives only the comparison and the result, without a full experimental configuration; below they are organized by what they aim to show, what they compare against and the result.

| Scenario | Compared against | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Agentic coding workload on Ironwood TPU (TPU 7x), prefix-aware routing + host-memory offload | Plain Kubernetes Service | Median TTFT down more than 85%, total throughput 2.4x |
| Gemini platform (formerly Vertex AI) production traffic through GKE Inference Gateway | Not stated in the blog | Prefix-cache hit rate from 35% to 70%; TTFT for coding agents down more than 35%; P95 TTFT under bursty chat traffic down more than 50% |
| 17,000-node multi-region GKE deployment across the US and Europe serving an MoE model | Not stated in the blog (result is for three clusters combined) | Combined throughput across three clusters scaled 2.9x (the blog gives no baseline; read literally, it is relative to one cluster), 99.9% request success rate, extra overhead from the routing layer below 1% (the blog does not say whether in latency or compute) |
| A3 Mega cluster serving a 70B model, 50k-token prompts, KV cache offloaded to both Managed Lustre and host memory | Offload to host memory only | TTFT improved about 40%, end-to-end latency down 30%, GPU-hour requirement down nearly 60% |
| Agentic coding workload test (IBM) | Upper limit of reusable cache | Counted in tokens, the prefix-aware router actually reused 97% of the prefix the workload could at most reuse (llm-d's own GLM-5.2 test reports 96–97%, e.g. a 91.4% hit rate against a 93.9% reusable ceiling) |
| 3,000 concurrent software-engineering agents, self-hosted deployment (IBM and Red Hat) | Buying the same open model as a service | Cost 5 to 10 times lower |

The first row answers how much cache-aware routing itself brings: on the same hardware, simply replacing round-robin with prefix-based routing and adding host-memory offload cut median TTFT by more than 85%. The second row is a check on production traffic: the prefix-cache hit rate doubled, consistent in direction with the drop in TTFT. The third row tests scale: routing overhead below 1% shows that the router's own computation did not become a bottleneck. The fourth row compares two KV-cache offloading schemes; with long 50k-token prompts, adding a shared storage tier has a clearer effect.

User reports show these components work in production. Snap reached prefix-cache hit rates of up to 75–80% with prefix-cache-aware routing. ZenteiQ raised daily generated tokens on the same number of TPU v6e accelerators from 1.47 billion to 5.97 billion, more than 4x higher aggregate throughput. Mistral uses flow control to enforce strict priorities across its commercial tiers, automatically holding or shedding lower-priority requests when pools saturate.

## 5. Limitations

The blog itself does not discuss limitations. Two facts need adding. First, most numbers in the table come with only a comparison and a result, so the baseline configuration, workload mix and measurement method need to be checked in the original sources linked from the blog. Second, many capabilities (GKE Inference Gateway's managed routing, cross-region failover, the Managed Lustre storage tier) are Google Cloud managed services, and on other clouds or self-built clusters you need to deploy the corresponding open-source components yourself.

## 6. Practical takeaways

- If you serve agents or multi-turn chat with vLLM or SGLang and still have round-robin load balancing in front, check the prefix-cache hit rate first. If it is low, prefix-based routing is the step with the smallest change and the most direct gain.
- When interactive requests and batch jobs share the same GPUs, flow control and async queues let batch jobs use only spare capacity, so interactive latency is not affected by batch work.

papers.title: SweepANN: A GPU-Accelerated Large-K Approximate Vector Search for Drug Discovery
papers.authors: Zhenyu Zhang, Qi Lin, Nan Zhang, Zhichao Cao
papers.summary: Drug screening needs hundreds of thousands of best-matching candidates from hundreds of millions of molecules for each protein pocket, and for such searches a full scan with a score cutoff beats building an approximate index. SweepANN splits the compressed molecule vectors across several GPUs, and one matrix multiplication scores a data block for a whole batch of pockets. The cutoff is set like this: each GPU first scans a few sample blocks and keeps, for each pocket, as many top-scoring molecules as will finally be returned. Merging across GPUs keeps the same number again, and the lowest of those scores becomes the cutoff, sent back to every GPU just once. After that only molecules above the cutoff are written into fixed-capacity buffers, and if a batch of pockets overflows, that whole batch is rescanned exactly. On four Blackwell GPUs, retrieving 500,000 candidates for each of more than twenty thousand pockets takes about 61 seconds once the library is in memory, with mean recall of 99.6% of exact search.
papers.abstract: DrugCLIP places small molecules and protein pockets in one space, turning genome-wide drug discovery into large-K retrieval by vector proximity. A campaign fixes over 20K pockets in advance for one library of over 500M molecules. Each pocket keeps K = 500K candidates, 0.1% of the collection, versus 100 in ANN benchmarks. Missed hits never get tested, so mean recall must reach 99% relative to exact search. SweepANN partitions compressed vectors across GPUs and scans each resident partition. One matrix multiplication scores each block for a whole query batch, reading it once. Four Blackwell GPUs answer all 26,562 pockets with a resident time of about 61 seconds, excluding library loading, and 99.6% mean recall relative to exact FP32 search. On 500M rows, the window plan runs 1.41x faster than SweepANN's grouped plan in the same memory. Across 25M-500M rows and K of 10K-500K, all GPU IVF configurations meeting the recall target take 8.2-24x SweepANN's resident time.

papers.title: llm-d 1.0 hardens open-source AI inference for production
papers.summary: Whether self-hosting open models for agents can cost less than buying a managed service comes down to cache reuse, because agent requests share large amounts of the same context. llm-d is an open-source inference stack built jointly by Google, IBM and Red Hat, and its stable release just shipped. It sends requests carrying the same context to the server that already holds that context, and lets the cache move between GPU, CPU and storage. IBM and Red Hat ran 3,000 coding agents at once at 5 to 10 times lower cost than a managed service. In another test, 97% of the reusable cache was actually reused.
papers.abstract: The distributed inference framework makes serving large models on your own infrastructure reliable and affordable for the agentic era. llm-d 1.0 focuses on day-two production operations for distributed inference.

papers.title: Amazon targets Trainium gains with new TorchNeuron developer tool
papers.summary: When moving to a new AI chip, the biggest cost is often not the hardware but rewriting and revalidating code. Amazon's new tool TorchNeuron lets existing PyTorch code run on its own Trainium chips by changing a single line of configuration. Amazon ran the same training script on conventional hardware and on Trainium, and the learning process behaved the same on both, showing that switching chips did not change the training result. The voice company Cartesia says its inference pipeline ran with almost no code changes; it only hand-wrote kernels for a few key layers that determine latency. Amazon is also contributing the related changes back to the official PyTorch codebase.
papers.abstract: TorchNeuron allows developers to run existing PyTorch code on AWS Trainium chips by changing one line of configuration. Amazon reports equivalent learning behavior between conventional hardware and Trainium while reducing hardware-specific changes, and is contributing upstream changes to PyTorch.

papers.title: FastLLM: a C++ LLM inference engine
papers.summary: For running a large MoE model without enough GPU memory, the C++ inference engine FastLLM lets weights be split layer by layer across GPU memory, CPU memory and even disk, but there is no benchmark data yet to check the speeds it advertises. The repository says it can run an unpruned DeepSeek model, without naming the version, on any GPU with more than 10 GB, and on a dual-socket server generate 20 tokens per second at full precision with one request at a time. It does not depend on PyTorch, reads weights straight from Hugging Face, and offers OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible APIs. The review notes that the repository has no releases and no benchmark file to check these figures against. Its niche is narrow: machines whose RAM or SSD is much larger than GPU memory and that need to run MoE models.
papers.abstract: FastLLM is a dependency-free, high-performance LLM inference library. On dual 9004/9005 servers with a single GPU, the full-precision DeepSeek model reaches 20 tokens per second, while the INT4 model reaches 30 tokens per second at single concurrency and more than 60 with multiple concurrent requests. It can place dense and mixture-of-experts layers across GPU, CPU, NUMA memory, and disk.

papers.title: Choosing a Vector Retrieval Database: The Built-in Vector Engine of Tair (Redis Enterprise Edition)
papers.summary: An Alibaba Cloud product-selection article argues that a RAG application already using Redis as a cache does not need a separate Milvus or Qdrant deployment and can use TairVector, the vector engine built into Tair, Alibaba Cloud's enterprise edition of Redis. It supports two indexes, the HNSW graph index, which is fast but approximate, and FLAT, which compares every vector for exact results. It combines vector search, BM25 full-text search and tag filtering in one query, keeps all data in memory and updates indexes in real time. The article says a single node reaches 510 thousand QPS on a performance-enhanced instance. A case study in the article says an e-commerce search team cut vector search latency from 15 ms to 3 ms after switching to Tair. The article also concedes that pure vector search beyond a billion vectors is still better served by a dedicated vector database. ==Teams already on Redis can drop a separate vector store, but very large data still calls for a dedicated one==.
papers.abstract: 向量检索是 RAG 和 AI 应用的核心基础设施，向量数据库选型直接影响系统复杂度和性能。文章介绍 Tair 内置向量引擎方案及其工程取舍，并报告单节点 51 万 QPS 的性能数据。

papers.title: Scaling LLM Inference via Parallelism: Throughput-Latency Trade-off
papers.summary: Should LLM inference use pipeline parallelism or tensor parallelism? This paper's conclusion is that it depends on how tight the first-token deadline is, not on throughput alone. The authors measured various parallel configurations on H200 and multiplied throughput by the share of requests that get their first token on time, giving the throughput that actually counts. When the deadline is very tight (5 to 10 seconds), pipeline parallelism, which assigns layers to different GPUs in order, is best; as the deadline loosens, the advantage shifts to tensor parallelism, which splits each layer across several GPUs that compute together. The longer the input, the more pipeline-heavy configurations come out ahead.
papers.abstract: This paper presents a systematic study of LLM inference parallelism from the perspectives of latency trade-offs, SLO-aware serving, and long-context scalability. It examines tensor, context, and expert parallelism and characterizes their communication and scaling behavior in distributed large language model inference.

papers.title: Introducing Superfluid: the local-AI native LLM server for multi-agent inference
papers.summary: When several agents run on one local machine, the request a person is waiting for in the chat box often queues behind batch work. Superfluid lets interactive requests jump ahead at the next scheduler tick, and in the launch blog's demo it answered about 30 times faster. In the demo, eight agents on one Mac are working through long documents when the user asks a question. Superfluid answers in 0.36 seconds, while llama-server with the same model takes more than 10 seconds. Servers like llama-server are built for throughput, so a new chat request waits behind running batches; Superfluid lets the agents' tasks resume afterwards. Requests that share a system prompt also get only one prefill. These figures come from a demo in the launch blog, not an independent benchmark. When several local agents share a machine, scheduling should put the request a person is waiting for first.
papers.abstract: Superfluid is an open-source Apache-2.0 server for running LLMs on your own machine. It supports the OpenAI, Anthropic and Ollama APIs and multiple runtimes, including llama.cpp for GGUF models, MLX for MLX directories, and the BaseRT engine for .base bundles.
